transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-10-05
Start time: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Thompson (Redwood AE), Ethan Li (Redwood SE), Priya Singh (Orchid Eng Mgr), Carlos Mendoza (Orchid Backend), Lena Park (Orchid Security)
Meeting title: SDK integration walkthrough - Orchid Commerce

Summary:
- Walkthrough of Redwood SDK quickstarts (Python + TypeScript), auth patterns, environment setup, and next steps for a short pilot.
- Discussed hosted vs dedicated options briefly; security questions flagged for follow-up (SOC2, KMS).

Topics:
- Python quickstart and env vars
- TypeScript client example and streaming responses
- Auth: API keys, SSO, service accounts, KMS for private deployments
- Quick local dev flow and CI integration
- Pilot benchmark and success criteria

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: hey everyone, thanks for joining, um this is Maya from Redwood, i'm the AE on the account. we've got Ethan on the call to do the SDK walkthrough, and then i think priya, carlos, lena from orchid. is that right?
[00:08] Priya: yeah that's right, hey maya, thanks for setting this up. we've been looking at Redwood for inference - mainly for our storefront personalization and support bot.
[00:16] Ethan: hey all, ethan here, i'll jump between the demo and some infra notes. quick note on timeline - you said you wanted a pilot in oct/nov?
[00:22] Priya: ideally by mid-november, yeah. we need low-latency for real-time recs, cost numbers, and SOC2 compliance details.
[00:30] Maya: perfect. demo plan is: show python quickstart, then ts example for streaming, auth patterns, env setup, and finish with how to run a small benchmark on dedicated vs hosted.
[00:39] Carlos: great, thanks. i'm mostly focused on the integration story - how messy is adding the client and rotating keys?
[00:45] Ethan: totally. we'll show the SDK flow and the recommended env var patterns; rotating keys is just standard -- we support short-lived service tokens when using our private control plane, and for hosted the API keys are revocable from the console.
[00:58] [00:58] Ethan: ok jumping into the python quickstart - i'm pulling up the repo link, note we'll share this after the call: https://github.com/redwood-inference/quickstarts (link to be sent)
[01:06] Ethan: sample pip install redwood-sdk, then set REDWOOD_API_KEY in your environment. example: export REDWOOD_API_KEY="sk_live_xxx". in code: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')). then client.generate(...).
[01:25] Priya: quick q - do you have first-party auth libraries for aws lambda or Google Cloud Functions? we want a minimal wrapper.
[01:32] Ethan: yes we have small adapters. the python lib plays nice in serverless. we also have a lightweight node lambda handler sample in the ts quickstart.
[01:40] Carlos: what about types - typescript types and auto-complete? our stack is node/ts.
[01:45] Ethan: full typings. for TS: npm i @redwoodai/sdk. example snippet: import { Redwood } from '@redwoodai/sdk'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY }); const stream = client.chat.stream({ model: 'redwood-1b', messages: [...] }); stream.on('data', chunk => { process.stdout.write(chunk.delta) });
[02:06] [02:06] Priya: streaming is important for UX. do you do chunked responses that keep latency low?
[02:10] Ethan: yes, the SDK surfaces streaming and we support chunked token delivery. also quick note: if you need ultra-low tail latency we recommend pinned dedicated capacity, but for most cases our hosted endpoints with prefix caching are sufficient.
[02:26] Lena: security question - we need to know how keys are stored and how logs are handled. do you ingest customer data?
[02:32] Maya: good one. short answer: for hosted, we retain request metadata per the retention policy; we can opt out of retention for enterprise plans. for private, you can keep everything in your VPC and we don't ingest it. we'll send SOC2 summary and the security questionnaire after.
[02:48] Lena: do you support KMS wrapping for keys? we use AWS KMS and HSM for production secrets.
[02:54] Ethan: yes - for private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM; for hosted we offer envelope encryption and can integrate with customer-managed keys for enterprise accounts. i'll flag that for the security follow-up.
[03:06] [03:06] Ethan: jumping back to the quickstart - env var suggestions: REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_DEFAULT_MODEL, REDWOOD_TIMEOUT_MS. for ci we recommend storing keys in your secrets manager and injecting at build time.
[03:20] Carlos: how do you recommend rotating keys in CI? like do you need service accounts per service?
[03:25] Ethan: best practice is per-service service tokens with limited scopes; we support token scopes and expiration. that way you can rotate without downtime.
[03:33] Priya: ok that sounds reasonable. can you show the node quickstart file layout?
[03:37] Ethan: sure - i pulled up the ts example: /examples/ts-chat/index.ts, package.json with scripts, .env.example. it shows how to do streaming and fallback logic. i'll paste the link in the chat after.
[03:48] [03:48] Maya: (typing) link dropped in chat: https://github.com/redwood-inference/quickstarts/tree/main/ts-chat
[03:53] Carlos: switching gears - what about model selection? you mentioned curated open models and redwood-verified performance. how do we pick for cost vs latency?
[04:00] Ethan: we usually start with a medium-sized open model, then run a small benchmark. Redwood Optimize will give suggestions on quantization and batching settings. for real-time recs, lower parameter models with quantization+dedicated capacity often hit latency SLOs with much lower cost.
[04:18] Priya: is there a programmatic API to get performance profiles?
[04:21] Ethan: yes, the console has profiles per model, and the SDK can fetch model metadata via client.models.list(). note: the auto-naming in the transcript might have turned that into client.models.least or something, but it's client.models.list() - we'll include exact snippets.
[04:38] Lena: for the pilot we need an audit log of requests and role-based access controls. is RBAC configurable per team?
[04:45] Maya: yes, RBAC is in the console - you can assign roles, restrict model access, and audit logs are exportable. for private deployments you get an enterprise-grade control plane and can ship logs to your SIEM.
[04:58] [04:58] Priya: quick technical: our traffic peaks at 1200 rps during promos. how does redwood handle batching vs latency?
[05:06] Ethan: good question. Redwood runtime does continuous batching with workload-aware batching windows. for strict tail-latency you can pin instances or use dedicated pools. we can run a small benchmark with a simulated traffic pattern. that's in the pilot template.
[05:22] Carlos: about cost - do you have per-token pricing for hosted? and how would dedicated be quoted?
[05:27] Maya: hosted is usage-based per token and per-embedding unit. dedicated is reserved capacity with a commit and we'd give a throughput-backed price. i'll include a ballpark in the follow-up and the pricing worksheet in the pilot packet.
[05:39] [05:39] Ethan: jumping back again - code example for error handling in ts: check stream.status, fallback to shorter context model, and instrument via our tracing hooks; we provide a middleware for open telemetry.
[05:52] Priya: ok, can you show the CI/CD flow for deploying the function that calls redwood? we need to see how secrets are injected and rotated.
[05:58] Ethan: sure briefly: 1) store key in secrets manager, 2) fetch at deploy time via pipeline, 3) set as REDWOOD_API_KEY env var. for ephemeral builds use short-lived tokens. we have a GitHub Actions example in the repo: .github/workflows/deploy.yml
[06:14] Lena: retention and deletion policies - if we opt-out of retention, how quickly is data deleted?
[06:19] Maya: we can do immediate deletion on request for enterprise plans; standard hosted has 30/90 day retention options. we'll provide the contract language.
[06:29] [06:29] Carlos: for the pilot, what's the minimum work from our side? we want to keep it low lift.
[06:34] Maya: minimum is: provision a sandbox account, run the quickstart for python or ts (5-10 min), run a small batch of requests per the benchmark template, then share logs. Redwood will run the same tests from hosted and optionally dedicated to compare metrics.
[06:48] Priya: good. we'll probably try ts first since our services are node-based.
[06:52] Ethan: makes sense. one note: if you want to test streaming in browser, we have a lightweight client example that proxies via a server to keep keys out of the browser.
[07:03] [07:03] Maya: ok, security follow-up - we'll send SOC2 summary, answers to your security questionnaire, and sample contract language. ethan will own KMS details.
[07:12] Lena: thanks. also please include info about network isolation for private deployments, and whether egress IPs can be fixed for firewall rules.
[07:20] Ethan: we can provide static egress IPs for dedicated/private and document the VPC peering options.
[07:27] [07:27] Carlos: small nit: is there an SDK example that uses the redis prefix cache? we use redis for caching and would love a demonstrated pattern.
[07:34] Ethan: yes, we have a caching pattern in the quickstarts; it's a prefix cache that stores KV tokens. i'll point you to the redis example.
[07:41] Priya: how long does the full pilot usually take? from our side to get meaningful numbers.
[07:45] Maya: usually 2-4 weeks: quickstart + basic benchmark in week 1, then a deeper run and cost analysis week 2-3.
[07:54] [07:54] Priya: ok that's doable. pricing and security are the gating items for procurement.
[07:59] Maya: understood. let's talk about specific SDK snippets i'll send - python minimal and ts streaming. then ethan will attach sample pipeline and pilot template.
[08:10] Ethan: sharing the pilot template verbally: test harness (k6 script or custom), request distribution (p50/p95/p99), sample payloads, success criteria (latency < 300ms p95, cost per 10k requests under $X), and env config.
[08:28] Carlos: can you dot the i's on the success criteria cost number? we need a rough estimate to show the CFO.
[08:33] Maya: i'll add a ballpark in the follow-up; exact depends on model choice and batching. we'll include a cost estimate for redwood-1b quantized vs a larger model on dedicated.
[08:45] [08:45] Priya: last question from me - how do we handle feature flags during rollout if a model quality regression happens?
[08:51] Ethan: our console supports rollouts and automatic fallbacks; you can set canary percentages and automatic fallback to a baseline model if quality dips. plus per-route metrics to monitor.
[09:03] Maya: alright we're at about 40 minutes. quick recap of next steps: maya to send SDK quickstarts + pricing sheet + security docs, ethan to send pilot template and benchmark scripts, priya to spin up sandbox account and try ts quickstart. any other questions?
[09:17] Priya: none from me, thanks.
[09:19] Carlos: all good. thanks both.
[09:21] Lena: thanks - looking forward to the SOC2 docs.
[09:24] Maya: thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email.

End of transcript.
